title: Effects of austempering on the microstructure and mechanical properties of high-strength nanostructured bainitic steel containing 3.5 wt% aluminum
abstract: This study aims to produce a cost-effective and low-density, high-strength nanostructured bainitic steel by optimizing the austempering process conditions. To do this, a steel containing 0.8C-1.5Mn-0.6 Cr-0.35Mo-3.5Al was selected and the effects of austempering time and temperature on the microstructure and mechanical properties of this steel were studied. Xrd technique was used to recognize the phases present in the microstructure and measure the retained austenite volume fraction and carbon content. Hardness measurements showed that the highest value was obtained from the specimen containing the highest volume fraction of the bainitic ferrite associated with the retained austenite with the highest carbon content, at the completion time of transformation. Such a combination of microstructure and hardness was applied to find the optimum time at different temperatures during the austempering process. The microstructures of the optimal specimens were evaluated through optical microscopy (OM) and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), and the average thickness of the bainitic ferrite plates was calculated. Finally, tensile tests were performed on the optimal specimens to assess the fracture surface through FESEM. For high steel with 3.5 wt% Al, the results indicated that it is possible to obtain a microstructure consisting of bainitic ferrite plates with an average thickness of 53 nm surrounded by the carbon-rich retained austenite with a hardness of 561HV, a yield stress of 1614 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 1981 MPa, and a total elongation of 9 %.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Bulk nanostructure materials are mainly obtained through either low-temperature phase transformation or plastic deformation [ 1 ]. Nanostructure Multi-phase steels, nano-pearlite, nano-martensite, microstructures with nanoparticles embedded within the matrix, and nanostructured bainite, also are produced in the same manner among which nano bainitic structures can be produced without additional plastic deformation [ 2 ]. Caballero and Bhadeshia introduced nanostructured bainitic steel as the first nanostructure bulk metal in the world [ 2 , 3 ]. This type of steel was reported to have a toughness of approximately 30 MPa m 0.5 , yield stress of 1300–1600 MPa, and an ultimate tensile strength of up to 2500 MPa. These mechanical properties resulted from a microstructure consisting of bainitic ferrite nano-plates separated by carbon-rich austenite regions [ 4 , 5 ]. The combination of nano-scale bainitic ferrite plates and the film-like carbon-rich retained austenite offers a useful range of properties for armor applications, bearings, and shafts and a promising substitution for the quenched and tempered steels [ 6–9 ]. Furthermore, the acceptable wear behavior of nanostructured bainitic steels has increased their potential for industrial applications [ 10 , 11 ].

However, the time-consuming formation of this microstructure remains a major challenge in the industrial mass production of nanostructured bainitic steels. For the first nanostructured bainitic steel, bainitic transformation at 125–350 °C required 2–60 days to be completed [ 3 ]. The bainitic transformation can be accelerated by increasing the temperature; however, this would increase the thickness of bainitic ferrite plates [ 12 , 13 ]. An increased free energy change of the austenite-to-ferrite phase transformation is the most effective method for accelerating bainitic transformation. In general, the microstructure can be modified at different temperatures during isothermal heat treatment by increasing the driving force of the transformation through two approaches [ 14 ]: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Encouraging the formation of large quantities of bainitic ferrite and removing the block-like retained austenite and 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Reducing the thickness of bainitic ferrite plates.

Al and Co increase the driving force of the bainitic transformation by increasing the free energy change of the austenite-to-ferrite phase transformation and accelerate the bainitic transformation. Moreover, Al and Co shift the

[ 19 ] replaced 1.68 wt% Co with 1.72 wt% Al in nanostructured bainitic steel and demonstrated that this replacement decreased the thickness of bainitic ferrite plates, increased the retained austenite volume fraction, reduced hardness and yield stress, and enhanced the ultimate tensile strength and total elongation.

Since Al has a negligible effect on austenite strength (only a 3 MPa reduction for 1 wt% Al), its presence can increase the driving force of transformation and decrease the thickness of bainitic ferrite plates. Al also reduces the density of steel used in the automotive industry. Hence, the high-strength nanostructured bainitic steels could benefit from this. As a result, Al could be useful for industrial applications, as it accelerates the bainitic transformation and decreases the steel density in light of its small atomic mass [ 20 , 21 ]. Hu [ 20 ] showed that the addition of 3.4 wt% Al to a high-carbon nanostructured bainitic steel decreased its density by 5.1 %.

Numerous studies have been conducted on the effects of Al on the nanostructured bainitic transformation for values below 2 wt%. The addition of Al above 2 wt% has not been reported in the literature [ 14 , 15 , 19 , 22–24 ]. This study sought to fill this research gap by evaluating the effects of 3.5 wt% Al on a high-carbon nanostructured bainitic steel to develop a substitute for conventional nanostructured bainitic steels, reduce the production cost by replacing Co with Al, reduce energy consumption by shortening the austempering time (accelerating the bainitic transformation through Al), and increase the attention for using such alloys in the automotive industry (by decreasing the total density in the presence of Al).

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
An alloy composition was selected to produce nanostructured bainitic steel with a lower density, production costs, and energy consumption than conventional nanostructured bainitic steels. Al and Co accelerate the bainitic transformation [ 14 , 15 , 18 , 25 ]. Co is an expensive alloy element and, as with Al, it accelerates the bainitic transformation [ 26 , 27 ]. Si decelerates the bainitic transformation [ 26 , 27 ] but prevents carbide formation, as with Al [ 28 , 29 ]. Therefore, 3.5 wt% aluminum was used to replace Si and Co to accelerate the process, enhance profitability, and reduce energy consumption in the fabrication of nanostructured bainitic steels. Furthermore, Al leads to a larger density reduction (smaller final weight) than the other alloy elements, which is another reason for this replacement [ 20 , 21 ]. As the Al value increases, the austenite stability region in the Fe–C diagram shrinks. Therefore, it is necessary to raise the carbon content of steel to obtain the all-austenite phase region [ 21 , 30–32 ]. For the Al value of 3.5 wt%, a carbon mass fraction of 0.8 wt% was selected. To lower the

The microstructure of nanostructured bainitic steels, especially the thickness of bainitic ferrite plates and the volume fraction of retained austenite, are influenced by the austempering conditions, particularly the temperature and holding time of austempering. Considering the obtained value for MS from quench dilatometry tests and the significant influence of temperature and holding time of isothermal treatments, various cycles were selected to investigate these two parameters. Initially, based on the fundamental concepts in nanostructured bainitic steels for producing nano-bains, an initial temperature slightly above MS temperature, 250 °C, was chosen. The samples were held in a salt bath for time intervals of 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h and then cooled in air. To investigate the effect of temperature and holding time of isothermal, the temperature was increased stepwise by 25 °C, and the samples were held in a salt bath for time intervals of 0.5, 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h and then cooled in air. sections.heading: Phase characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          shows the XRD patterns of specimens austempered under different conditions. According to  Fig. 3 (a) and (b), in the specimen austempered at 250 °C and 275 °C bainitic ferrite and retained austenite appear after 3 h, while these phases are present in the microstructure after 1 h in the specimens austempered at 300 °C and 350 °C. According to  Fig. 4 
                         (a), an increase in the austempering time reduced the retained austenite volume fraction, regardless of the temperature, with the transformation approaching its completion and a higher bainitic ferrite volume fraction. However, the increment rate of bainitic ferrite volume fraction declined. In longer periods, bainitic ferrite content slightly increased, and the bainitic ferrite volume fraction remained almost unchanged in the final microstructure. An increase in the austempering time increased bainitic ferrite plate growth and induced a larger plastic strain in the initial austenite phase; as a result, the dislocation density in austenite increased [ 2 , 42 , 43 ]. This raised the autocatalytic nucleation sites and led to the formation of new bainitic ferrite subunits and further austenite decomposition into bainitic ferrite [ 44–46 ]. Moreover, an increased austempering time decreased the austenite available for transformation into bainitic ferrite, reducing the increment rate of the bainitic ferrite volume fraction. A rise in the austempering time also accelerated bainitic transformation completion. An increased temperature reduced the activation energy of C atom diffusion, raising bainitic ferrite nucleation and bainitic ferrite volume fraction and accelerating the transformation. At the same time, the increased austempering temperature reduced the driving force of nucleation due to undercooling reduction and, therefore, grain-boundary nucleation site reduction, reducing the number of initial nuclei for the formation of bainitic ferrite. At the same time, the increased C atom diffusion at the higher austempering temperatures increased the carbon content of austenite. Hence, the carbon content reached the

                          curve and the bainitic transformation was discontinued faster. This diminished the bainitic ferrite volume fraction and increased the retained austenite volume fraction at the time of transformation completion at the higher austempering temperatures.

According to  Fig. 4 (d), an increase in the austempering time raised the carbon content of retained austenite and decreased the carbon increment rate, regardless of the temperature. At the longer austempering times, the carbon content of retained austenite rose slightly and then remained almost unchanged. As the austempering time and austenite decomposition into bainitic ferrite increased, more carbon was distributed from the tips of the subunits into austenite, raising the carbon content of retained austenite. The increased austempering time and, thus, reduced bainitic transformation rate decreased the number of new subunits. Since C atoms were distributed into austenite from the subunit tips, the reduced bainitic transformation rate and subunit formation rate at an increased austempering time decreased the increment rate of carbon content, and the carbon content remained almost unchanged at the higher austempering times. Furthermore, the increased austempering temperature increased the carbon content of retained austenite. The increased austempering temperature raised the bainitic transformation rate due to the increased diffusion of C atoms and led to further C atom distribution into the retained austenite. Therefore, the carbon content of retained austenite increased as the austempering temperature increased.

sections.heading: Hardness measurement
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          shows the hardness versus the logarithmic time at different austempering temperatures. A rise in the austempering time reduced hardness to a minimum level, regardless of the austempering temperature. A further increase in the austempering time increased hardness, with hardness remaining almost unchanged at long times. Moreover, the hardness increment rate decreased as the time increased above the minimum hardness time, regardless of the austempering temperature. At short austempering times, hardness was high due to the martensite phase of the microstructure; however, as the austempering time increased, due to increased retained austenite stability under martensite transformation upon the increased carbon content of the retained austenite at longer times, the martensite content of the microstructure increased, and bainitic ferrite increased due to further bainitic transformation, leading to a hardness reduction. Once hardness was minimized at a given temperature, martensite disappeared in the microstructure. A further increase in the austempering time raised hardness by increasing the bainitic ferrite volume fraction due to further bainitic transformation, and hardness remained almost unchanged at the longer austempering times due to the completion of the bainitic transformation. Furthermore, the increased austempering time reduced the austenite content available for transformation into bainitic ferrite, reducing the increment rate of the bainitic ferrite volume fraction and the hardness increment rate.

An increased austempering temperature reduced hardness, regardless of the austempering time. The strength of nanostructure bainitic steels had an inverse relationship with the average thickness of bainitic plates. As the austempering temperature increased, the average thickness of bainitic ferrite plates increased, leading to a steel strength reduction [ 47–49 ]. Furthermore, the increased carbon content of retained austenite enhanced the mechanical stability of retained austenite. As a result, a rise in the average thickness of bainitic ferrite plates and the carbon content of retained austenite because the increased austempering temperature diminished hardness.

sections.heading: Optimization
paragraphs:
Based on the quantitative and qualitative microstructural evaluations and hardness values under austempering conditions, the shortest reasonable time to obtain the maximum bainitic ferrite volume fraction and the maximum carbon content of retained austenite with maximum hardness (bainitic transformation completion time) was selected as the optimal time at a given austempering temperature.  Table 2 
                          reports the optimal times at different austempering temperatures along with quantitative evaluations. According to  Fig. 6 
                         (a), an increase in the austempering temperature increased the thickness of bainitic plates and also hardness due to the decreased austenite resistance to the advance of the bainitic ferrite-austenite interface and reduced density of dislocations in the austenite. Furthermore, the increased carbon content of retained austenite because of the increased austempering temperature enhanced the mechanical stability of the austenite and diminished hardness ( Fig. 6 (b)).

Fig. 7 
                         (a–d) shows the optical microscopy (OM) images of the microstructures obtained from different austempering conditions. Accordingly, the microstructure consisted of bainitic plates and a block austenite phase, and an increase in the austempering temperature increased the retained austenite. The rising temperature increased the carbon content of retained austenite by raising C atom diffusion. As a result, the carbon content of the retained austenite intersected with the

Fig. 7 (e–h) demonstrates the FESEM images of a higher resolution. Accordingly, the microstructures of all the specimens consisted of thin nano-scale bainitic plates surrounded by the retained austenite films.

According to  Fig. 11 
                         , the fracture surfaces of all specimens consisted of dimples, cleavage facets, and river lines. The number and diameter of dimples increased as the austempering temperature rose. An increased austempering temperature raised the retained austenite volume fraction and the average thickness of bainitic plates, decreasing strength, enhancing ductility, and inducing a ductile failure tendency ( Figs. 9–10 ). This, in turn, increased the number and diameter of dimples.

Fig. 12 
                          compares the proposed steel with the Steel of other researchers in terms of tensile properties [ 50 ]. The tensile properties of specimens that austempered at 250 °C for 24 h, 275 °C for 18 h, and 300 °C for 12 h were within the ranges of bainitic steels reported in the earlier works.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
The production cost, energy consumption, and density of bainitic steels can be reduced by replacing expensive Co with Al to develop the industrial applications of nanostructured bainitic steels. Furthermore, a yield stress of 1464–1614 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 1753–1981 MPa, and a total elongation of 9.12–14.12 % can be obtained by changing the austempering temperature at an austempering time of 12–24 h. Finally, from the isothermal transformation of austenite to bainite in the steel of this study, the following results were drawn: 
                         
                            1 
                            Increasing the austempering time at any bainitic transformation temperature increases the residual austenite carbon content due to the increase of austenite decomposition into bainitic ferrite. However its rate of increase decreases due to the decrease in the rate of bainitic transformation, and when the transformation stops, the remaining austenitic carbon content does not change significantly. Also, with the increase in the austempering temperature, due to the increase in the diffusion of carbon atoms, the carbon content of the remaining austenite increases. 
                         
                         
                            2 
                            In fully bainitic samples, increasing the austempering time by increasing the volume fraction of bainitic ferrite increases the hardness value. However, the rate of hardness increase decreases due to the decrease in the available amount of austenite for transformation into ferrite during austenite transformation, and at the end of the transformation, the hardness value becomes almost constant. 
                         
                         
                            3 
                            Increasing the austempering temperature by increasing the average thickness of the bainite ferrite plates and increasing the mechanical stability of the remained austenite due to the increase in the carbon content of the remaining austenite causes a decrease in hardness. 
                         
                         
                            4 
                            Increasing the austempering temperature on the one hand by decreasing the parameter
